items.title: Locally integrable functions as regular distributions
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice for the published embedding theorem. For open Ω⊂ℝⁿ, n≥1, the regular distribution T_u(φ)=∫Ωuφ is attached to the almost-everywhere class [u]∈L¹_loc(Ω). The map [u]↦T_u is complex linear and injective; test pairings are bilinear, without conjugation.
items.strategy: Use the published regular-functional definition for finiteness and the published locally-integrable embedding theorem for the injection and its Countable Choice hypothesis. Keep the latter as a cited interface, not a new proof of FA-24.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3

items.title: Weak derivative of a locally integrable function
items.statement: For u,v∈L¹_loc(Ω) and α∈ℕ₀ⁿ, v is D^αu weakly if ∫ΩuD^αφ=(−1)^|α|∫Ωvφ for every φ∈C_c^∞(Ω). The test identity itself is choice-free. Equivalently D^αT_u=T_v in the published distribution convention; assuming Countable Choice for regular-distribution injectivity, α=0 says v=u almost everywhere.
items.strategy: Define the test identity first and identify both sides with regular distributions using the signed-transpose definition. Every test has compact support, so both integrals are finite. Under Countable Choice apply the published regular-distribution injection for the α=0 equivalence.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3

items.title: Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. If u,ũ and v,ṽ are locally integrable and u=ũ, v=ṽ almost everywhere, then v=D^αu weakly if and only if ṽ=D^αũ weakly. This applies to L^p classes, 1≤p≤∞, since they are locally integrable on Euclidean open sets.
items.strategy: For each compact test support, almost-everywhere equality preserves both integrals. To include arbitrary L^p representatives, bound their local L¹ norms by Hölder against the indicator of the finite-measure support; at p=∞ use the essential bound times its measure. No point value enters.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3

items.title: Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. If v,w∈L¹_loc(Ω) both satisfy the weak α-derivative identity for the same u, then v=w almost everywhere on Ω.
items.strategy: Subtract the two test identities, so the regular distribution T_(v−w) vanishes on every test. Apply the published injection of L¹_loc classes into distributions. This proves uniqueness on the whole open set, including disconnected Ω.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3

items.title: Classical derivatives agree with weak derivatives
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. If u∈C^k(Ω;ℂ), k≥0, then for |α|≤k the classical ∂^αu is locally integrable and is D^αu weakly.
items.strategy: Use compact-support integration by parts coordinate by coordinate, exactly as in the published classical-compatibility clause for regular distributions; boundary terms vanish because the test is compactly supported. Translate ∂^αT_u=T_(∂^αu) back to the weak identity and invoke uniqueness for its a.e. class.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3

items.title: Linearity, locality, and commutation of weak derivatives
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Weak derivatives are linear in their locally integrable inputs; a weak derivative restricts to any open V⊂Ω. If D^αu and D^βu have locally integrable representatives, existence of any one of D^β(D^αu), D^α(D^βu), or D^(α+β)u as a locally integrable weak derivative implies existence of the other two and equality of all three.
items.strategy: For linearity and restriction, use the defining test identity. For commutation, apply the published equality of distributional derivatives, then use regular-distribution injectivity to identify all function-valued representatives. The qualification on existence avoids inferring an unrepresented derivative.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3

items.title: Zero weak gradient gives componentwise constants
items.statement: Assume AC. Let Ω⊂R^n be open with n≥1, 1≤p≤∞, and K∈{R,C}. If u∈W^(1,p)_loc(Ω;K) has Du=0 almost everywhere, then u is almost everywhere constant on each connected component of Ω; when Ω is empty the claim is vacuous.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (Aalto University, 2026)
references.locator: Chapter 2 §2.6, Remark 2.38(4), printed p. 59; the connected-domain result is stated as an ACL exercise, without proof.

references.title: MATH 712 Real Analysis Solutions to Take-home Midterm, Spring 2016, Part B
references.locator: Exercises 1–2, PDF pp. 3–4, and Exercise 7, PDF p. 8; its local mollification and countable-union argument are completed here with explicit overlap compatibility.

items.strategy: On nested balls whose doubled closures lie in Ω, zero extend each local restriction and mollify it. The mollifications have zero gradients and are constant on the inner balls; L1 convergence gives local almost-everywhere constants. Overlaps define a locally constant value, connectedness makes it constant on each component, and a countable rational-ball cover plus countable subadditivity gives the global almost-everywhere conclusion.

items.title: Weak Leibniz rule with a smooth factor
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. If η∈C^∞(Ω), u∈L¹_loc(Ω), and every D^γu with γ≤α has a locally integrable representative, then D^α(ηu)=Σ_(β≤α) binom(α,β)(D^βη)D^(α−β)u as an L¹_loc class. If u∈W^(k,p)(Ω) and η and its derivatives through k are bounded, the formula also holds in L^p; compactly supported η is a sufficient global condition.
items.strategy: On compact test supports, all η derivatives are bounded and each product is locally integrable. Apply the published distributional Leibniz identity to T_u, identify multiplication by η with T_(ηu), and use injection for the function-valued formula. For the global clause use bounded multipliers on each Lp derivative.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3

items.title: Integration by parts for dual-exponent Sobolev functions
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let Ω⊂ℝⁿ be open, n≥1, 1≤p≤∞, and p′ the conjugate exponent (1′=∞, ∞′=1). For complex- or real-valued u∈W^(1,p)(Ω), v∈W^(1,p′)(Ω), if at least one a.e. class is zero almost everywhere outside a compact K⊂Ω, then ∫Ω u D_i v=−∫Ω v D_i u for every i. The bilinear integrals are absolutely convergent, including both endpoints. The original full-AC hypothesis is weakened to its countable fragment, which is all the proof uses.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (Aalto University, 2026)
references.locator: Chapter 1 §1.7, Theorem 1.19, printed pp. 17–18; finite-p local mollification and convergence in the Sobolev norm.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
references.locator: Chapter 3 §3.4, Theorem 3.19, printed pp. 55–56; mollified weak derivatives and local L1 convergence.

items.strategy: Define compact support for a.e. classes. Use locality to show the weak derivative vanishes off the same compact set, extend the compactly supported factor by zero, and mollify it strongly in each finite L^r. Pass its smooth-test identity by Holder. In the only uncovered endpoint case, where the compact factor is in W^(1,∞), cut off and mollify the W^(1,1) partner, then pass using endpoint Holder; never approximate strongly in W^(1,∞). The proof uses only Countable Choice interfaces.

items.title: Restriction and smooth cutoff are bounded on Sobolev spaces
items.statement: Assume AC. For k∈N₀ and 1≤p≤∞, restriction W^(k,p)(Ω;K)→W^(k,p)(U;K) to an open U⊂Ω is contractive in the inherited norm. If η∈C_c^∞(Ω;K), multiplication by η is bounded W^(k,p)(Ω;K)→W^(k,p)(Ω;K), with its operator norm controlled by the finitely many sup norms of D^βη for |β|≤k. The proof uses AC only to invoke Countable Choice interfaces for weak-derivative uniqueness, the Sobolev quotient norm, and smooth-factor Leibniz.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapter 1 §§1.2–1.3
references.locator: Lemma 1.14(4)–(5), printed pp. 9–11 (PDF pp. 11–13); restriction and smooth-factor Leibniz formula

items.strategy: Use weak locality to restrict each derivative and monotonicity of the integral (or the essential-bound definition) to contract each Lp norm. Apply the weak smooth-factor Leibniz formula, bound every finite-sum term by the corresponding derivative sup norm, and take the finite Sobolev p-sum or maximum. Compact support and continuity make all cutoff derivative sup norms finite. AC supplies the CC assumptions of the cited interfaces.

items.title: Sobolev functions paste across an overlap
items.statement: Assume AC. If Ω=U∪V with U,V open and u_U∈W^(k,p)(U), u_V∈W^(k,p)(V) agree almost everywhere on U∩V, they paste to a unique u∈W^(k,p)(Ω) whose weak derivatives restrict to those of both pieces; its global norm is bounded by the two local norms (by their sum when p=∞).

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (Aalto University, 2026)
references.locator: Chapters 1–3, especially §§1.1–1.4, 2.2, 2.6 and 3.1–3.5

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
references.locator: Chapter 3 §§3.1–3.5

items.strategy: Use local equality of a.e. classes on the overlap and uniqueness/locality of weak derivatives. For a compactly supported test, choose a finite smooth partition subordinate to U,V, apply each local weak derivative identity and cancel cutoff derivative terms. This proves the global distribution identity. Since this is a two-open cover, each pasted derivative has finite global L^p norm bounded by the sum of its two local norms. Do not extend the same bound to an arbitrary infinite cover without summability.

items.title: Integer-order Sobolev spaces and their norms
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice for derivative-class uniqueness and representative independence. For open Ω⊂ℝⁿ, k∈ℕ₀, and 1≤p≤∞, W^(k,p)(Ω;𝕂) is the set of 𝕂-valued L^p a.e. classes whose weak D^αu has an L^p representative for every |α|≤k, with D^0u=u. For p<∞ set ||u||_(W^(k,p))=(Σ_(|α|≤k)||D^αu||_p^p)^(1/p); for p=∞ set ||u||_(W^(k,∞))=max_(|α|≤k)||D^αu||_∞. Here 𝕂 is ℝ or ℂ; all derivatives use bilinear tests.
items.strategy: Under Countable Choice use the preceding representative-independence and uniqueness results to assign each derivative class. The finite index set is all multi-indices of order at most k; at k=0 this is Lp. Define local W^(k,p) by membership on every relatively compact open subdomain when needed.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3

items.title: The Sobolev norm descends to equivalence classes
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice for the weak-derivative uniqueness interface. The displayed W^(k,p) formula is independent of representatives and is a norm: it is finite, homogeneous, subadditive, and zero exactly on the zero Lp class, for 1≤p≤∞ and real or complex scalars.
items.strategy: Use representative independence and uniqueness to make every derivative class intrinsic. Derive linearity of the derivative vector locally or cite the earlier linearity lemma. For finite p, apply Lp Minkowski componentwise, then apply integral Minkowski on the finite multi-index set with counting measure; for p=∞ take the maximum of the componentwise bounds. Homogeneity follows from the Lp quotient norm axioms. Since α=0 occurs, norm zero forces ||u||p=0 and hence u=0 as an Lp class.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3

items.title: Integer-order Sobolev spaces are Banach
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice, used to invoke the published real and complex Lp completeness results and choose representatives of component limits. For every open Ω, k∈ℕ₀, 1≤p≤∞, and 𝕂∈{ℝ,ℂ}, W^(k,p)(Ω;𝕂) is complete for its displayed norm.
items.strategy: A Sobolev-Cauchy sequence is Cauchy in Lp in every derivative coordinate. Use the published Lp completeness to obtain component limits v_α, with v_0=u. For each compactly supported test, local finite measure and Hölder (L∞ paired with L1 at the endpoint) pass ∫u_jD^αφ=(−1)^|α|∫D^αu_jφ to the limit. Thus v_α=D^αu weakly; convergence of the finite coordinate array is Sobolev-norm convergence. Explicitly check k=0 and the zero domain.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
Haim Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations (2011), Chapter 8 §8.2

items.title: Weak lower semicontinuity of the Sobolev norm
items.statement: Assume AC. If 1<p<∞, k∈N₀, and u_j converges weakly to u in W^(k,p)(Ω), then ∥u∥_(W^(k,p))≤liminf_j ∥u_j∥_(W^(k,p)).

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (Aalto University, 2026)
references.locator: Chapters 1–3, especially §§1.1–1.4, 2.2, 2.6 and 3.1–3.5

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
references.locator: Chapter 3 §§3.1–3.5

items.strategy: Apply the published weak lower-semicontinuity theorem to the Banach space W^(k,p)(Ω). Equivalently use weak continuity of each derivative map into L^p and lower semicontinuity of the finite product norm. Preserve the exact finite-sum norm convention from the W^(k,p) definition.

items.title: The notation Hk and the reserved zero-boundary symbol
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice for the cited W^(k,2) equivalence-class interface. For integer k≥0 define H^k(Ω;K):=W^(k,2)(Ω;K), with the same a.e. classes and weak derivatives. The symbol H^k_0(Ω) is reserved for the later Sobolev closure definition; this item does not define it by pointwise boundary values or assert an equality to any trace-zero set.
items.strategy: Use the established integer-order W^(k,2) equivalence-class space and norm. Reserve H^k_0 for the later closure definition; do not assign boundary representatives or infer a trace characterization.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3 §3.5
references.locator: Definition 3.23, printed p. 59 (PDF p. 63)

items.title: Hk has the derivative-sum Hilbert inner product
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice for the cited L2 completeness. On H^k(Ω;ℂ), ⟨u,v⟩_(H^k)=Σ_(|α|≤k)∫ΩD^αu overline(D^αv) is a well-defined inner product linear in the first variable; in the real case omit conjugation. Its induced norm is exactly the displayed W^(k,2) norm, and H^k is complete.
items.strategy: Each L2 pairing is representative-independent and finite by complex Cauchy–Schwarz. Sum the finitely many inner-product axioms; α=0 gives positive definiteness. The squared induced norm is Σ||D^αu||²_2, exactly the Wk2 formula, so Banach completeness from the preceding theorem makes it Hilbert.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3
Haim Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations (2011), Chapter 8 §8.2

items.title: Weak derivatives persist under local Lp limits
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let 1≤p,q≤∞. If u_j→u in L^p_loc(Ω), D^αu_j→v in L^q_loc(Ω), and every indicated derivative exists, then D^αu=v weakly. In particular a sequence of Sobolev derivatives with these limits has the expected unique limiting class.
items.strategy: For a fixed test with compact support K, local finite measure and Hölder turn both Lp convergences into L1 convergence against D^αφ and φ. Pass the weak identity to the limit. Use uniqueness to identify v as a class; no almost-everywhere convergence of the full sequence is assumed.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3

items.title: Weak differentiation has a closed graph on its natural domains
items.statement: Assume AC. Let n≥1, 1≤p≤∞, K∈{R,C}, and Ω⊆R^n be open. The full weak gradient D:W^(1,p)(Ω;K)⊆Lp(Ω;K)→(Lp(Ω;K))^n has a closed graph when the finite product has the maximum norm. For each i, the maximal partial derivative D_i:V_i→Lp, V_i={u∈Lp:D_i u exists weakly with value in Lp}, is also closed. If n≥2, every restriction D_i|W^(1,p)((−1,1)^n;K), considered with the ambient Lp domain norm, is not closed, for each p and i; explicit witnesses cover finite p and p=∞. AC is used only through ACω for the cited Sobolev, weak-stability, measure, and sequential-closure interfaces.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (Aalto University, 2026)
references.locator: Chapter 1 §1.4, Theorem 1.15 and completeness proof, printed pp. 11–13; proof passes weak test identities for 1<p<∞ and leaves p=1,∞ estimates as exercises.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
references.locator: Chapter 3 §3.4, Theorem 3.20 and complete proof, printed p. 56; local L1 weak-derivative limit criterion, not the global Lp closed-graph or single-coordinate failure claims.

items.strategy: Pass graph limits to the weak test identity using the earlier local weak-stability lemma, coordinate by coordinate for the full gradient and on the maximal domain for a partial derivative. Show a partial derivative restricted to W^(1,p) is not closed by smooth approximations of a transverse jump for finite p and of |x_k|^(1/2) for p=∞; the limits are outside W^(1,p). The sequences require n≥2 and an explicit coordinate distinct from the differentiated one.

items.title: Absolute continuity on almost every coordinate line
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice for the completed-product Fubini convention. An a.e. class u on open Ω has an ACL representative if some measurable u*:Ω→𝕂 equals u a.e. and, for each coordinate direction i, outside a null set of transverse parameters on every relatively compact rational coordinate box, its restriction to every compact segment of the corresponding line in Ω is absolutely continuous. One common u* must work for all i; exceptional lines may differ with i.
items.strategy: State the quantified representative property on a countable box basis, so exceptional sets can be united without requiring a claim about every section of an arbitrary Lebesgue-measurable representative. Identify Euclidean Lebesgue measure with the completed product for Fubini; absolute continuity is componentwise for complex values.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapter 2 §2.6
references.locator: Theorem 2.36 (Nikodym, ACL characterization), statement printed p. 55 and proof pp. 56–59

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3
references.locator: §3.A.2, Definition 3.56, printed pp. 78–79, for absolute continuity on compact intervals

items.title: ACL line derivatives reconstruct weak gradients
items.statement: Assume AC. Let Ω⊂R^n be open, n≥1, 1≤p≤∞, and K∈{R,C}. Let u∈L^p_loc(Ω;K) have one measurable ACL representative u*, and suppose measurable functions g_i∈L^p_loc(Ω;K) satisfy: on almost every line parallel to the i-th coordinate axis, the one-dimensional derivative of the ACL section of u* exists and equals the section of g_i almost everywhere. Then g_i is the weak derivative D_i u for every i.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapter 2 §2.6
references.locator: Theorem 2.36, converse proof, printed p. 59 (PDF pp. 60–61)

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3 §3.5
references.locator: Definition 3.23 and weak derivative convention, printed p. 59 (PDF p. 63)

items.strategy: For each compactly supported test, use a smooth locally finite partition subordinate to rational coordinate boxes and retain its finite part. On one box, apply one-dimensional AC integration by parts on almost every good coordinate line. Local Lp and finite box measure put each test product in L1; completed-product Fubini and the Euclidean completion identity give the weak identity. AC is used only to invoke the CC and DC hypotheses of those cited interfaces.

items.title: ACL characterization of W1p
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice, used for the cited completed-product Fubini and one-dimensional absolute-continuity FTC interfaces. For 1≤p<∞, a real or complex a.e. class u belongs to W^(1,p)(Ω) if and only if u∈Lp(Ω) has one ACL representative u* whose classical coordinate derivatives exist almost everywhere, are measurable, and belong to Lp(Ω). In that case D_i u equals ∂_i u* a.e. for every i.
items.strategy: Forward: local W1p is local W11 on compact boxes. Convolve the regular distribution with one fixed smooth approximate identity on its safe domains; the published distribution convolution identity makes ∂i u_ε=(D_i u)*ρ_ε. A compact cutoff and the published L1 approximate-identity theorem give local L1 convergence of u_ε and every ∂i u_ε. Choose one decreasing rational ε_j with summable W11 differences on the first j rational boxes. Completed-product Fubini makes the sums of linewise L1 derivative differences finite on almost every line in every direction. On a compact subsegment, ||h||∞≤|I|^(−1)||h||L1(I)+||h′||L1(I); therefore the smooth restrictions converge uniformly and their derivatives converge in L1. The common pointwise limit u* is AC on those lines and equals u a.e.; its line derivatives equal D_i u a.e. Converse: apply the one-dimensional AC FTC and integration by parts to u*φ on good lines, then completed-product Fubini; the resulting distribution identity gives each weak derivative. All exceptions are united over finitely many directions and countably many boxes.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
Haim Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations (2011), Chapter 8 §8.2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3

items.title: One-dimensional Sobolev functions have unique AC representatives
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and AC-FTC interfaces. If I⊂ℝ is an open interval and u∈W^(1,p)(I), 1≤p≤∞, then exactly one continuous representative u* on I is locally absolutely continuous and u*(x)−u*(y)=∫_y^xD u(t)dt for every x,y∈I. If I=(a,b) has finite endpoints, u* extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on [a,b], with u*(x)=u*(a)+∫_a^xD u for every x∈[a,b].
items.strategy: For finite p apply ACL in one dimension. For p=∞ apply it on every bounded subinterval after local inclusion into finite-p Sobolev; patch continuous representatives on overlaps by a.e. equality. The one-dimensional AC FTC gives the integral formula. On a bounded interval Du∈Lp⊂L1, so its integral has finite endpoint limits and supplies an AC extension. Two continuous functions equal a.e. agree everywhere because a nonzero continuous difference has an open nonnull set.

references.title: Haim Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations (2011), Chapter 8 §8.2
Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2

items.title: Chain rule for a C1 function with bounded derivative
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL interface. Let 1≤p≤∞, u∈W^(1,p)(Ω;ℝ), and F∈C¹(ℝ;ℝ) with ||F′||∞<∞. Then F∘u∈W^(1,p)_loc(Ω) and D_i(F∘u)=F′(u)D_i u a.e. It belongs to global W^(1,p)(Ω) exactly when F(u)∈Lp(Ω); the latter is automatic if F(0)=0, if Ω has finite measure for finite p, or for p=∞.
items.strategy: Take the common ACL representative, using local finite-p membership when p=∞. On a good line u* is AC; F is globally Lipschitz, so F∘u* is AC. At a.e. point where u* is differentiable, the ordinary C1 chain rule yields F′(u*)∂i u*. The gradient has local and global Lp bound ||F′||∞||D_i u||p. Apply the ACL converse on compact boxes, then use the displayed global integrability condition; F(0)=0 gives |F(u)|≤||F′||∞|u|.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3

items.title: Chain rule for globally Lipschitz scalar maps
items.statement: Assume AC. Let u∈W^(1,p)(Ω;R), 1≤p≤∞, and F:R→R be globally Lipschitz. Then F(u)∈W^(1,p)_loc(Ω), and it lies in global W^(1,p)(Ω) whenever F(u)∈L^p (in particular when F(0)=0). Almost everywhere D_iF(u)=F′(u)D_i u where F is differentiable at u; on the remaining preimage take the product as zero because Du=0 almost everywhere there.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (Aalto University, 2026)
references.locator: Chapters 1–3, especially §§1.1–1.4, 2.2, 2.6 and 3.1–3.5

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
references.locator: Chapter 3 §§3.1–3.5

items.strategy: On almost every ACL line, F∘u is AC and the one-dimensional Lipschitz chain rule applies. Rademacher gives differentiability of F off a null set; prove the AC line derivative vanishes almost everywhere over the preimage of that null set by the one-dimensional area/change-of-variables identity, then F′(u)u′ is valid with the stated zero convention. Fubini reconstructs each weak derivative. The Lipschitz bound controls |DF(u)|; |F(u)|≤Lip(F)|u| when F(0)=0 gives global L^p. For p=∞, apply the local finite-p ACL argument on bounded boxes and then use the global L∞ bounds for F(u) and its gradient.

items.title: Positive, negative, and truncated Sobolev functions
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice for the preceding chain rule and ACL result. For real u∈W^(1,p)(Ω), 1≤p≤∞, u⁺,u⁻,|u| and T_Mu=min(M,max(−M,u)), M≥0, belong to W^(1,p)(Ω). Almost everywhere D_i u⁺=1_{u>0}D_i u, D_i u⁻=−1_{u<0}D_i u, D_i|u|=sgn(u)D_i u with zero on {u=0}, and D_iT_Mu=1_{|u|<M}D_i u with zero on the two level sets.
items.strategy: Choose the C1 Lipschitz approximation P_ε(t)=0 for t≤0 and P_ε(t)=sqrt(t²+ε²)−ε for t>0. Its derivative is zero on t≤0, bounded by one, and tends to 1_{t>0}; derive t⁻ from (−t)⁺ and |t|=t⁺+t⁻. Apply the smooth-composition chain rule and dominated convergence in each test pairing, or the weak-stability lemma, to identify the derivative. The positive/negative identities imply D_i u=0 a.e. on {u=0}; apply this to u±M for the clipping levels. Apply the positive-part formula locally to u−M and −M−u (which need not be globally Lp on an infinite-measure domain); their positive parts are bounded by |u| and so are globally Lp. Express T_Mu=u−(u−M)⁺+(−M−u)⁺ and use |T_Mu|≤|u| for global Lp.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3

items.title: Sobolev maxima and minima form a lattice
items.statement: Assume AC. For real u,v∈W^(1,p)(Ω), 1≤p≤∞, both u∨v and u∧v lie in W^(1,p)(Ω). Almost everywhere D_i(u∨v)=1_{u>v}D_i u+1_{u≤v}D_i v and D_i(u∧v)=1_{u<v}D_i u+1_{u≥v}D_i v; on {u=v} the two gradients agree almost everywhere.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (Aalto University, 2026)
references.locator: Chapters 1–3, especially §§1.1–1.4, 2.2, 2.6 and 3.1–3.5

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
references.locator: Chapter 3 §§3.1–3.5

items.strategy: Write u∨v=v+(u−v)^+ and u∧v=u−(u−v)^+. Apply the positive-part gradient formula to u−v. The existing level-set identity gives D(u−v)=0 almost everywhere on {u=v}, so either tie convention yields the same a.e. gradient.

items.title: Weak derivatives are represented distributional derivatives
items.statement: Under the Countable Choice convention for the regular-distribution injection, D^αu is a weak derivative exactly when the distribution ∂^αT_u lies in the image of L¹_loc(Ω)→D′(Ω); then its function class is uniquely determined. A distributional derivative always exists, but a Dirac mass or another singular distribution need not have a locally integrable representative, so not every Lp function has an Lp weak derivative.
items.strategy: Compare the defining signed test pairings and use the injectivity theorem for the unique class. For δ₀, shrinking unit-height smooth tests have constant δ₀ pairing but their pairings with any L1loc function tend to zero by absolute continuity of the integral, so δ₀ is not regular. The companion later gives the explicit step witness without serving as a proof dependency here.

references.title: Haim Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations (2011), Chapter 8 §8.2
references.locator: Printed p. 203, Examples (exercise (ii)) and Remark 3; the step-function assertion is posed as an exercise, while Remark 3 states the distributional-derivative criterion for W^{1,p}

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3
references.locator: Chapter 3 §3.2, Example 3.4, printed pp. 48–49; computes the step derivative and proves no L¹_loc representative

title: Weak Derivatives and Sobolev Spaces — Examples

items.title: The absolute value has a weak first derivative
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. On any bounded open interval I containing 0, u(x)=|x| belongs to W^(1,p)(I) for every 1≤p≤∞. Its weak derivative class is represented by v(x)=−1 for x<0 and +1 for x>0, with any finite real value at x=0.
items.strategy: For a real test φ, set G=|x|φ and g=sgn(x)φ+|x|φ′; use the product rule off {0} and finite-exception Newton–Leibniz to obtain the weak identity. Convert the Riemann identity to Lebesgue integrals, bound u and the derivative representative on the finite-measure interval for finite p and p=∞, and use the null singleton to vary the value at 0.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
references.locator: Chapter 1 §1.1, Example 1.7, printed pp. 2–3 (fully worked piecewise-affine test calculation); Chapter 2 §2.2, Theorem 2.3, printed pp. 29–31 (absolute-value rule for 1≤p<∞, with smooth approximation and dominated convergence)

references.title: Haim Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations (2011), Chapter 8 §8.2
references.locator: Chapter 8 §8.2, Examples (i), printed p. 202; the exact |x| claim on (-1,1) for 1≤p≤∞ is posed as an exercise without proof

items.title: Absolute value has a Dirac second derivative
items.statement: On R, D²|x|=2δ_0 in distributions. Hence |x|∈W^(1,∞)_loc(R) but |x|∉W^(2,1)_loc(R).

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (Aalto University, 2026)
references.locator: Chapters 1–3, especially §§1.1–1.4, 2.2, 2.6 and 3.1–3.5

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
references.locator: Chapter 3 §§3.1–3.5

items.strategy: For φ∈C_c^∞(R), split ∫|x|φ″ at zero and integrate twice on each half-line. Boundary terms at infinity vanish and the jump of the first derivative from −1 to +1 contributes 2φ(0). A Dirac mass is not an L¹_loc function class.

items.title: A step has no locally integrable weak derivative
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let I=(−1,1), K∈{R,C}, and H=1_{(0,1)}. Then H∈L^p(I;K) for every 1≤p≤∞. Its regular distribution satisfies ∂T_H=δ₀ in D′(I), but no v∈L¹_loc(I;K) represents this derivative. Consequently H∉W^{1,p}(I;K) for every 1≤p≤∞.
items.strategy: For every test φ, −∫Hφ′=φ(0), the Dirac pairing. If v∈L1loc represented it, take φ_ε(x)=η(x/ε) with η(0)=1 and support shrinking to {0}; absolute continuity of the L1 integral makes ∫vφ_ε→0, whereas δ₀(φ_ε)=1. This contradiction does not rely on pointwise derivatives away from the jump.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3 §3.2
references.locator: Example 3.4, printed pp. 48–49; the shrinking-test proof makes the locally integrable obstruction explicit

items.title: Cantor function has singular distributional derivative
items.statement: The Cantor staircase on (0,1) is continuous and locally constant, hence absolutely continuous, on each complementary interval of the null Cantor set, but it is not in W^(1,1)(0,1): its distributional derivative is the nonzero singular Cantor measure.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (Aalto University, 2026)
references.locator: Chapters 1–3, especially §§1.1–1.4, 2.2, 2.6 and 3.1–3.5

items.strategy: Use the standard Cantor staircase: it rises from 0 to 1 while its classical derivative is zero almost everywhere. If its weak derivative were an L¹ function, the one-dimensional W^(1,1) AC representative theorem would force endpoint change equal to the integral of that derivative, hence zero, contradiction. Distributionally the derivative is the probability measure of the Cantor construction. Cite Kinnunen Examples 2.35 and its ACL theorem for the exact obstruction.

items.title: Sharp Sobolev threshold for a radial power
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let n≥1, a>0 and, for arbitrary finite c∈R, u(0)=c and u(x)=|x|^(−a) off 0 on B(0,1). For every finite 1≤p<∞, u∈Lp iff ap<n and u∈W^(1,p;R) iff p(a+1)<n; in the Sobolev range D_i u is represented off 0 by −a x_i|x|^(−a−2). In all dimensions u∉L∞ and hence u∉W^(1,∞;R).
items.strategy: Use Borel measurability and the polar-coordinate formula to reduce the Lp and candidate-gradient integrals to one-dimensional power integrals. Prove the exact integrability threshold by dyadic annuli and geometric series. For sufficiency when p(a+1)<n, use a shrinking smooth cutoff around 0; the omitted function, omitted gradient, and cutoff-product errors are O(ε^(n−a)), O(ε^(n−a−1)), and O(ε^(n−a−1)), all tending to zero. For necessity, restrict any Lp weak derivative to the punctured ball, identify it with the classical derivative by compatibility and uniqueness, and use polar divergence. Essential unboundedness on every small punctured ball excludes L∞; n=1 has no finite-p Sobolev range.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (Aalto University, 2026)
references.locator: Chapter 1 §1.2, Example 1.10, printed pp. 6–7; off-origin derivative, punctured-ball boundary estimate, and 1≤p<n W1p threshold

items.title: Subcritical W1p is not closed under multiplication
items.statement: Let n≥2 and 1≤p<n. On B_1 choose a smooth cutoff χ near zero and α with (n/p−1)/2≤α<n/p−1. Then u(x)=χ(x)|x|^(−α) belongs to W^(1,p)(B_1), while u² does not.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (Aalto University, 2026)
references.locator: Chapters 1–3, especially §§1.1–1.4, 2.2, 2.6 and 3.1–3.5

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
references.locator: Chapter 3 §§3.1–3.5

items.strategy: The radial derivative of u has singular order r^(−α−1), whose pth power is integrable iff p(α+1)<n. The derivative of u² has order r^(−2α−1) and its pth power diverges when p(2α+1)≥n. The chosen interval satisfies both inequalities; smooth cutoff terms are harmless.

items.title: Matching pieces across a hyperplane have no jump derivative
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let n≥2 and Q=(−1,1)^n. For K=R or C, let f_± be C¹ up to the boundary on the closed half-boxes [−1,1]^(n−1)×[0,1] and [−1,1]^(n−1)×[−1,0], with matching traces on (−1,1)^(n−1)×{0}. Then their piecewise function f is in W^(1,p)(Q;K) for every 1≤p≤∞, and D_j f is represented a.e. by the corresponding piecewise classical partial derivative.
items.strategy: Bound f and each derivative on the compact half-boxes and prove their Borel measurability by finite gluing; the box formula gives finite measure and hence all Lp endpoints, including p=1 and p=∞. For the normal derivative, apply finite-exception Newton–Leibniz to f(y,t)φ(y,t); continuity at t=0 is exactly trace matching. For each tangential derivative, apply the same one-dimensional identity along x_j-lines away from the null parameter set x_n=0. Convert the bounded Riemann section integrals to Lebesgue integrals, use the completed-product measure identification and Fubini, and conclude the weak identities.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (Aalto University, 2026), Chapter 1 §1.1
references.locator: Example 1.7, printed pp. 3–4; complete one-dimensional piecewise-affine test calculation

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3
references.locator: §3.2, Example 3.3, printed p. 48; one-dimensional positive-part test calculation

references.title: Haim Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations (2011), Chapter 8 §8.2
references.locator: §8.2, Examples (i) and following sentence, printed pp. 202–203; one-dimensional exercises

items.title: A hypersurface jump is not W1p
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. On Q=(−1,1)^n, n≥2, u(x)=1_{x_n>0} lies in every Lp(Q), but its distributional normal derivative is surface integration against the coordinate hyperplane {x_n=0}; it has no L¹_loc representative. Thus u∉W^(1,p)(Q) for every 1≤p≤∞.
items.strategy: Take tensor tests φ(y,t)=ψ(y)η(t) with ∫ψ=1. Direct integration gives −∫u∂_nφ=η(0), the same normal Dirac functional as the one-dimensional step. If a locally integrable normal derivative existed, shrink η(t/ε) while keeping ψ fixed; absolute continuity of the integral over the shrinking slab would force the pairing to zero, contradiction. Tangential derivatives are zero and do not remove the normal obstruction.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3

items.title: Lp and Sobolev classes do not determine point values
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. On any nonempty Euclidean open Ω, choose x₀∈Ω. The zero function and the function equal to 1 at x₀ and 0 elsewhere represent the same element of every Lp(Ω) and W^(k,p)(Ω), all k≥0 and 1≤p≤∞, although their values at x₀ differ. Therefore evaluation at x₀ is not a well-defined operation on these equivalence classes.
items.strategy: The singleton {x₀} is Lebesgue null. The two measurable representatives agree a.e., so their Lp classes, weak test pairings, all derivative classes, and Sobolev norms coincide by representative independence. Their displayed point values differ, proving failure of class-level evaluation.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3
Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2

items.title: Point evaluation is unbounded below the Sobolev continuity threshold
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let n≥2, let Ω⊆R^n be open with 0∈Ω, let K∈{R,C}, and let 1≤p≤n. There is a sequence of real-valued K-valued test functions u_m∈C_c∞(Ω;K) such that sup_m ||u_m||_{W^(1,p)(Ω;K)}<∞ and |u_m(0)|→∞. Thus point evaluation at 0 is unbounded on C_c∞(Ω;K) in the W^(1,p) norm; no bounded linear functional on W^(1,p)(Ω;K) agrees with ordinary evaluation on every test function.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (Aalto University, 2026)
references.locator: Chapter 1 §1.2, Examples 1.11–1.12, printed pp. 8–9; those examples exhibit unbounded W^{1,p} functions in the stated exponent regimes but do not prove the smooth-test-sequence or point-evaluation claim, which is derived explicitly here.

items.strategy: For 1≤p<n, use shrinking compactly supported smooth bumps whose values at the origin grow linearly while the Lp norms of the function and gradient decay by scaling. For p=n≥2, use an explicit logarithmic radial cutoff made smooth by the flat smooth step; polar integration bounds each gradient norm and both the core and annular L^n terms while its value at the origin grows. The sequences rule out every bounded linear extension of point evaluation.

items.title: A clipped affine function keeps its zero region
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice for the cited Sobolev truncation calculus. Let M>0 and Q=(−2M,2M)^n. The function w(x)=min(M,max(0,x₁)) belongs to W^(1,p)(Q) for every 1≤p≤∞. It is zero on {x₁≤0}, equals x₁ on {0<x₁<M}, and equals M on {x₁≥M}; its weak gradient is e₁ on the middle slab and 0 elsewhere, with interface values irrelevant.
items.strategy: The affine x₁ is smooth and bounded on Q, so it belongs to every W1p. Apply positive-part calculus to x₁ and x₁−M, writing w=(x₁)⁺−(x₁−M)⁺. Subtract the two weak gradients. Both zero and plateau regions have gradient zero; the interfaces are null and the corner calculus has already established their level-set behavior.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces (2026), Chapters 1–2
John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014), Chapter 3
